summary: Updates the IETF Anti-Harassment Procedures in RFC 7776 to reflect that the IAOC was replaced by the IETF Administration LLC and the Administrative Director by the Executive Director. It also removes updates that RFC 8713 already incorporated.

eli5.summary: A rule about treating people kindly named some job titles that no longer exist. This fixes the names so the rule still makes sense.

subtitle: Updating IETF harassment procedures to reflect changes in governance structure.

tldr.problem: The IETF Anti-Harassment Procedures (RFC 7776) refer to the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) and an Administrative Director, both of which no longer exist after the IETF reorganized and created the IETF Administration LLC.
tldr.mechanism: This document replaces references to the IAOC with the IETF Administration LLC and the Administrative Director with the IETF LLC Executive Director in RFC 7776. It also removes an update to RFC 7437 because that update has been incorporated into RFC 8713.
tldr.outcome: The anti-harassment procedures now accurately reflect the current IETF governance structure. The document is lightweight but essential for keeping procedural documents in sync with organizational reality.

today: RFC 8716 is an active Best Current Practice that updated RFC 7776 in February 2020. The IETF Anti-Harassment Procedures now correctly reference the IETF Administration LLC and the IETF LLC Executive Director, and the redundant update to RFC 7437 has been removed. The fairness protections and procedures for handling harassment remain the IETF's foundation for a respectful community.

sections.title: Why This Update Is Needed
sections.content:
The IETF Anti-Harassment Procedures, defined in RFC 7776, establish rules for how the IETF community should be treated fairly and how harassment concerns are addressed. These procedures are essential guidance that affects the day-to-day functioning of the organization.

However, the IETF recently restructured its governance. The IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC)—which handled budget and administrative oversight—was replaced by a new structure called the IETF Administration LLC. The Administrative Director position was replaced by an Executive Director role. RFC 7776 still used the old names, making the document outdated and confusing.

This document updates RFC 7776 to use the current names and organizational structure, ensuring that the anti-harassment procedures are clear about who is responsible for what.
sections.eli5: The IETF had an old committee called the IAOC. That became the IETF LLC with a new leader. The anti-harassment rules still said IAOC, so this fixes them.

sections.title: The Organizational Transition
sections.content:
Before this change, the IETF was governed by a structure that included the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee. This committee oversaw the IETF Secretariat, managed the budget, and provided administrative oversight of the organization's operations.

The IETF reorganized to create the IETF Administration LLC, a more streamlined structure led by an Executive Director. This change simplified governance and made decision-making clearer. However, procedural documents that referenced the old structure became unclear.

The key insight is that nothing fundamentally changed about the anti-harassment procedures themselves—the rules, remedies, and processes remain the same. Only the names of the committees and positions needed updating.
sections.eli5: The IETF reorganized its management structure, but the rules for treating people well stayed the same. This just updates the names.

sections.title: Changes to Training Budget Consultation
sections.content:
The IETF Anti-Harassment Procedures require the IETF Chair and the Ombudsteam (the group that handles harassment complaints and ensures fair treatment) to consult on training for the Ombudsteam itself.

Before this update, RFC 7776 stated: "the IETF Chair and Ombudsteam shall take professional advice and will consult with the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) with respect to the overall IETF budget."

After this update, it now reads: "the IETF Chair and Ombudsteam shall take professional advice and will consult with the IETF Administration LLC with respect to the overall IETF budget."

This is a direct name substitution. The process and the principle—that training decisions should be made in awareness of budget constraints—remain identical.
sections.eli5: When the Ombudsteam plans training, they talk with the budget people. The old rule said IAOC; the new one says IETF LLC. That is the only change.

sections.title: Changes to Remedy Enforcement
sections.content:
When the Ombudsteam determines that a remedy is needed to address harassment or unfair treatment, they must sometimes ask the IETF Secretariat or a leadership figure to take action.

The old text in RFC 7776 said: "the Ombudsteam will make a request in writing to the IETF Secretariat and/or IETF Administrative Director (IAD) to take action as appropriate."

The updated text now says: "the Ombudsteam will make a request in writing to the IETF Secretariat and/or IETF LLC Executive Director to take action as appropriate."

Again, this is a straightforward name change. The Ombudsteam still has the authority to request action, and the Executive Director still has the responsibility to respond—the change reflects who currently holds that title.
sections.eli5: When the Ombudsteam asks for help enforcing a fairness decision, they write to the IETF leader. That leader used to be called the Administrative Director; now it is the Executive Director.

sections.title: Cleaning Up Updates to RFC 7437
sections.content:
RFC 7776 originally updated RFC 7437, which describes the IETF Nominating Committee (NomCom) and the recall process for IETF leadership. Specifically, RFC 7776 had added a provision allowing the Ombudsteam to initiate a recall petition without gathering 20 community signatures—a significant power given to the Ombudsteam.

However, when RFC 8713 was published (also in February 2020), it obsoleted RFC 7437 and incorporated the Ombudsteam update into itself. This means the update from RFC 7776 is now redundant; RFC 8713 already has the correct language.

To avoid confusion, this document removes the outdated update reference from RFC 7776. The RFC's metadata will no longer say it updates RFC 7437, and relevant text in RFC 7776 is trimmed. The recall provisions the Ombudsteam needs are now clearly stated in RFC 8713.
sections.eli5: RFC 7776 used to fix something in an older rule (RFC 7437). But a newer rule (RFC 8713) replaced that old rule and already had the fix. So this removes the redundant update.

sections.title: Outcome and Impact
sections.content:
This is a small but important update. RFC 8716 is Best Current Practice (the same level as RFC 7776 itself) and came out in February 2020, ensuring that the IETF's anti-harassment procedures reflected the actual organizational structure shortly after the IETF Administration LLC was established.

For anyone reading RFC 7776 to understand the IETF's commitment to fairness and the procedures for addressing harassment, this update ensures clarity: the documents name the current committees and leadership roles, not phantom entities that no longer exist. The substance of the anti-harassment procedures—the Ombudsteam's role, the types of remedies available, the training requirements—remains unchanged and continues to protect the IETF community.
sections.eli5: This is a housekeeping update: name changes so the rules make sense with today's IETF structure. The fairness rules themselves did not change.

Kucherawy, M., Ed., Hinden, R., Ed., and J. Livingood, Ed., "IAB, IESG, and IETF LLC Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Operation of the IETF Nominating and Recall Committees", RFC 8713, February 2020.
